meta.description: Not Carl Jung. The line comes from John W. Gardner's 1964 book Self-Renewal; Jung is a modern misattribution with no source.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Creative minds are rarely tidy'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Carl Jung. It first appears in John W. Gardner's 1964 book Self-Renewal, per Quote Investigator. No Jung source exists.

answer.label: Not Carl Jung — actually John W. Gardner
answer.authorDates: 1912–2002 · U.S. reformer, Carnegie Corporation president & founder of Common Cause
answer.sourceLine: The earliest documented instance is John W. Gardner’s 1964 book Self-Renewal: The Individual and the Innovative Society, where he writes “Creative minds are rarely tidy” with no attribution to anyone else, per Quote Investigator ↗. There is no evidence Carl Jung ever wrote or spoke this line — the Jung credit is a modern internet invention.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Self-Renewal: The Individual and the Innovative Society

trail: Quote Investigator ↗ locates the earliest instance in John W. Gardner’s Self-Renewal (1964), pages 49 and 69–70, used with no attribution to anyone else.
QI reports the saying is credited online to Carl Jung and others but finds no historical evidence for any of those attributions — the Jung credit is a later error.
Later variants swap “rarely” for “seldom” (office signs and magnets from the late 1990s onward), but the original 1964 wording is “rarely tidy.”
source.excerptNote: Gardner applied the same idea to groups, writing that creative organizations or societies are “rarely tidy” as well — a point Quote Investigator ↗ documents from the same book.
source.rightsHolder: Estate of John W. Gardner / HarperCollins (successor to Harper & Row)
source.rightsNote: The line was first published in John W. Gardner’s Self-Renewal (Harper & Row, 1964). As a work first published in 1964 by an identifiable author and publisher, it is in copyright in the United States; rights rest with Gardner’s estate and the publisher’s successor, HarperCollins.

author.metaLine: 1912–2002 · U.S. public official & reformer; author of Self-Renewal
author.bio: John William Gardner (1912–2002) was an American writer and reformer who served as U.S. Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare, led the Carnegie Corporation, and founded the citizens’ lobby Common Cause. His best-known book, Self-Renewal (1964), argued that people and institutions must keep renewing themselves to stay creative — the context in which the “rarely tidy” line first appears.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: The line is endlessly shared as Carl Jung wisdom — on posters, prints, and social media — but no one has ever produced a Jung source for it.

items.why: Jung is the most common credit online, but Quote Investigator ↗ found no evidence he wrote or said it; it appears in none of his documented works and postdates the phrasing’s real 1964 origin.
A common modern form reads “Creative minds are seldom tidy.” QI dates this swap to office signs and magnets from the late 1990s; Gardner’s 1964 original reads “rarely tidy.”

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented source is John W. Gardner’s Self-Renewal (1964), where he used it as his own observation — not Carl Jung, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it stuck to Jung
lead: The saying is a tidy aphorism about the messiness of creativity — exactly the kind of clever, feel-good line that gets pinned on a famous psychologist. Carl Jung, with his reputation for probing the creative unconscious, is a magnetic but unsupported host for it.
The real author, John W. Gardner, wrote it in a 1964 book about renewal in individuals and institutions, applying “rarely tidy” to creative people, organizations, and whole societies alike.
context.pull: A clever line about mess — ironically, its own attribution is a mess.
